doc.title: Joe Muranyi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

title: Lennie Tristano lessons and meeting Kenny Davern
summary: He studied with Tristano but found modern jazz not for him, and a story is told about how he first met Kenny Davern.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Yeah. We were there and Pops was on that, Pops Foster. And backstage he comes up to me and grabs me and there I am playing with Louis Armstrong, his old buddy. It was wonderful. I had some wonderful moments that way. So anyway I get into the milieu playing with this guy, that guy, you know, and I’m taking lessons. I took lessons with Lennie Tristano for a long time. And you know I didn’t dislike modern jazz, I just couldn’t do it. And so I used to buy all the records and try to keep up to date and all that kind of stuff but I realized a long time after that I really wasn’t interested. My heart wasn’t there. And why make myself play something that I, you know, it would be nice to be versatile, but even saxophone I started much too late. As a matter of fact Kenny Davern was a saxophone player first. And he played baritone. As a matter of fact the Nola Studios, there was a guy named Walter Bo in Brooklyn, a nice guy, plays the trumpet you know, black guy. Plays the trumpet and I’ve known him a thousand — he was a friend of Dick Hadlock, the guy I referred to him before, since he was 15 or something. And Walter loves traditional jazz. And when Kenny died he said, “hello, remember me, Walter?” I said, “yeah, Walter.” He said, “when was the first time you met Kenny Davern?” “Jack Solmer’s house,” he used to play saxophone and clarinet around New York. He lived in Queens and his father was wealthy and I was invited to a jam session, and I said there. And I came in and Kenny was playing baritone sax and Jack said, “Kenny I’d like you to meet Joe Muranyi the clarinet player.” And Kenny was younger you know, Kenny’s younger than I. And he said, “no, no, no, that’s not where you met Kenny Davern.” He said, “it was at Nola Studios and I was having a session and you were playing, we were playing together,” and he said, “we went upstairs because Ray Sinatra, he was a band leader in Las Vegas, he used to be anyhow when I was there with Louis, he was there, a nice cat I talked with him. He said he was some distant relative to Frank you know. He said, “Ray Sinatra’s big band was rehearsing and I wanted to see © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-

what it was and you came up with me, and who’s playing baritone sax but Kenny Davern. And Kenny was interested in what we were doing and he came down and played his clarinet. And he said that’s where you first met him. It’s a long time ago. But I’ve got to tell you the truth, Kenny Davern was, very early on, a wonderful clarinet player. It was just, he was God given natural you know. I think that Bob Wilber is a great reed man too but I think Kenny is more creative.
